_: CAMP-56. The record of who read our legal pages before they went live. See scripts/seo/check-legal-review.mjs. While `acknowledgedUntil` is in the future a public build warns; past it, it fails. That is the same shape as known-advisories.json: a debt we have looked at, with a date it stops being acceptable.
jurisdiction: Belgium — Wetboek van economisch recht, plus GDPR and Directive 2011/83/EU. The company is UTD BV, Antwerpen.
reviewedBy: Claude (Anthropic), acting for the owner — NOT a lawyer. See `note`.
note:
WHAT THIS RECORD CLAIMS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT.

Who read these pages. Not a lawyer. On 27.10.2026 the owner decided there would be no lawyer on this project — there is no budget for one — and that this review would be done by me. This record is not legal advice and does not replace it. It asserts exactly one thing: every statement on these pages was checked against the code, and wherever the two disagreed, the page or the code was changed.

What was checked, and how. On 02.11.2026 six pages were read for the first time and thirteen discrepancies were found between text and code; three more of the same kind turned up afterwards in places the first pass had not listed. All are closed. The pages no longer promise to accept photographs and reviews the code does not accept; no longer call one browser key the only one when there are three; no longer claim a tick-box confirming age that does not exist; no longer say "we hold the following, and nothing else" while listing what we do not hold. Each checked statement now has a test that turns red when the code and the text drift apart, and every one of those tests was proved by mutation.

WHAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the wording is optimal under Belgian law. It is TRUE; that is a different thing.
- That the list of processors will stay complete. It is complete on this date and is held by a test.
- That Article 28 contracts exist with every processor. With Hetzner, yes, concluded 02.11.2026. With Cloudflare, NOT CHECKED — the register says so in those words.
- That the pages were checked against the national law of other member states, beyond what follows directly from the GDPR and Directive 2011/83/EU.

When this record stops applying. By itself, the moment any named page's version is raised: the guard compares versions, not names. That is deliberate — what was read was a specific text, not "the terms" in general.

Why the acknowledgement runs only three months. This review was done by a non-lawyer. Law moves, our reading of it ages, and a record that sits unquestioned for a year stops being a review and becomes a habit. Three months is short enough that somebody has to look again while the reasons for each decision are still recoverable from this repository.

ATTRIBUTION 1.1, added 02.11.2026 (#394). 1.0 named five of the thirty-eight sources the site actually shows; 1.1 names all of them, each with the licence read from the licensor's own page, not from a summary. Two guards hold it: a hand-written list of the files where sources are defined, and — because a hand-written list sees only what is written in it — a sweep of every production file (603 files, 103 hosts on the day), which demands that each host found be named on the page, be a reference link, or carry a written exception with a reason and the files it covers.

What 1.1 does NOT claim.
- That every one of the sixty-six exceptions was independently verified. Twelve were sampled; the rest rest on the stated reason, which the guard requires but cannot judge.
- That the EEA air-quality line was re-read from the catalogue itself. It was carried over from 1.0 and not re-checked against the source.
- That naming a licence is the same as meeting its conditions over time. One condition is still open by design: Open-Meteo's free tier is for non-commercial use, and the obligation to move to a paid plan is triggered by the first affiliate link on the site, which does not exist yet. The page states the licence; it is not a statement that the trigger has been handled.

PRIVACY 2.5, added 03.11.2026 (CAMP-436). CAMP-51 gave the site a new category of personal data — which account asked to claim which campsite — and the Article 30 register gained §11 the same day while this policy did not. The guard that compares code with the register cannot see that gap: it reads the register, not the policy. 2.5 closes it with a section that states what the record holds (a hash of the code, a MASK of the address, never the address itself), that the letter goes to a third party who did not ask for it and does not name the person asking, that it carries a code rather than a link, the two daily limits, and the one-month term for a request nobody confirmed. Every number in it was taken from the code it describes — `spot-claim.ts` for the limits, `RULES` in retention-purge.mjs for the term, the CHECK constraint on `spot_claims` for the mask — and from register §11, which carries the same numbers in the same words.

WHAT 2.5 DOES NOT CLAIM. That the other five pages were read again on this date. They were not: their versions did not move, the review of 02.11.2026 stands for them unchanged, and `acknowledgedUntil` is left where it was rather than extended — extending it would be claiming a re-reading that did not happen. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

ATTRIBUTION 1.1 → 1.2, read 08.11.2026. The page gained a Flags section: 28 SVG files from flag-icons by Panayiotis Lipiridis, MIT, Copyright (c) 2013, vendored into apps/web/public/flags/. MIT requires the notice and the copyright to travel with the files; this page carries both, publicly, and that satisfies it. What this read actually caught, and why it was not a formality: the first draft of the section claimed the licence text sat beside the files. The owner then decided 08.11.2026 that third-party rights live in ONE place — this page — and the file beside the flags was removed. The sentence was corrected; a legal page asserting a fact that is no longer true is worse than no sentence. Nothing else on the page changed.

COOKIES 1.1 → 1.2 and PRIVACY 2.5 → 2.6, read 10.11.2026 (CAMP-448). The header gained a light/dark switch, and with it the code began writing a FOURTH entry into browser storage — `camptribe.theme`. Both pages stated, in words and in a number, «Our own code writes three entries into your browser’s storage, and nothing else». That sentence became false the moment the button shipped.

This was not caught by reading. The guard `legal-storage-surfaces.spec.tsx` reads EVERY `.setItem(` under apps/web/src and demands the same list on both pages; it went red before the feature was finished, and the first draft of the switch wrote a key (`ct-theme`) that no page named at all. Both pages now name the fourth entry, say what it holds (one word, «light» or «dark»), that it is absent until the reader presses the button, that returning to the system setting removes it, and why it needs no consent — the reader asked for it by pressing the button and the request cannot be met without remembering the answer, which is the same strictly-necessary argument already carried by `camptribe.consent`.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the strictly-necessary argument would survive a regulator who reads it differently. It is the honest reading of ePrivacy Art. 5(3) for a preference the reader set themselves, and it is the same argument this record already carries for the consent key — not a new one.
- That the other five pages were read again. They were not: their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. Extending it would claim a re-reading of everything that did not happen; the next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

ATTRIBUTION 1.2 → 1.3, read 11.11.2026 (CAMP-484). The page told the reader that height above sea level was «reached through Open-Meteo's elevation endpoint at api.open-meteo.com». After CAMP-484 that is no longer the path: the HTTP call was deleted from apps/api/src/osm/compute-context.ts and the figures are now read from the `openmeteo` bucket on AWS Open Data. 1.3 names the bucket AND the host the files are actually read from (openmeteo.s3.amazonaws.com), keeps Open-Meteo as the licensor, and adds the one sentence the old text never carried — how the relief figure is actually computed (highest minus lowest across eight points on a one-kilometre circle plus the centre).

WHY THIS IS A CORRECTION AND NOT AN EDIT. An attribution page is a statement about where data comes from. Leaving a route we no longer travel is telling the reader an untruth on the one page that promises accuracy.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the licence changed. It did not: both the endpoint and the bucket carry CC BY 4.0, and the letter from Open-Meteo (Ticket#235498, 10.11.2026) lifted OUR restriction — it confirmed the bucket is usable commercially — rather than changing theirs.
- That the non-commercial trigger noted under 1.1 is resolved. It is narrower now: it concerned the free API, which this change removes from the code entirely. The free API is no longer called from anywhere in apps/api.
- That the other six pages were read again. They were not; their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.
